newsitem.title: INDIA: Strong global dollar bends before the Indian rupee.
newsitem.headline: Strong global dollar bends before the Indian rupee.

text.p: The U.S. dollar, surging against major global currencies, was fighting a losing battle against the Indian rupee on Monday, dealers said.
The rupee ended the day a shade weaker after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened in the market, buying dollars to push the rupee to close at 35.72/73 against a 35.71/72 opening.
The dollar had closed at the latter level on Friday after the RBI intervened when the Indian currency broke through the crucial 35.70-mark to trade at 35.69.
The market was looking to the RBI from early Monday morning but dollar purchases by the State Bank of India (SBI), India's largest bank, helped hold the dollar at the 35.71/72 level.
SBI's dollar purchases usually move the thin Indian foreign exchange market.
After SBI withdrew from the market, the rupee eased to 35.7050/7100, threatening to test the 35.70-barrier, provoking RBI's entry, dealers said.
RBI bought unspecified amounts of dollars upto the 35.73 level, dealers said. On Friday too, RBI purchases had pushed the rupee to 35.72/73 before closing at 35.71/72, they said.
"The (dollar) supplies were heavy today," said the treasurer of a European bank in Bombay.

India's leading truck maker Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company is raising $200 million in overseas debt and two Indian telecommunications firms are about to begin road shows to tap the global capital market.

Foreign institutional investors (FII) continue their purchases on Indian bourses. On July 10, FIIs' net purchases on the Bombay Stock Exchange alone amounted to 80 million rupees, according to latest data released by the exchange.
"The RBI has decided to put the dollar on 'intervention oxygen' only in extreme cases," said a dealer.

Indian exporters have been crying themselves hoarse about an overvalued rupee hurting their competitiveness but the government is helpless in the face of unabated capital flows into the country, dealers said.
"The forex market has become a graveyard for dealers," said a dealer at a European bank in Bombay. "If the fundamentals are so strong, they should allow the rupee to strengthen," he said.
"Otherwise the RBI should open a dollar purchase window," he said. He said the central bank's current unannounced interventions left most banks groping in the dark.
"Such intervention does not help anyone," he said.
The six month annualised forward dollar premium closed the day at 3.52 percent, down from the previous close of 3.63 percent.
